fr:title.text: Directory-based coherence scales by replacing broadcasts with point-to-point messages

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Directory-based coherence scales by replacing broadcasts with point-to-point messages

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A scalable Cache coherence organization for systems too large for a shared bus. Each memory address has a home node; the home node maintains a directory entry listing which caches currently hold copies and in what state. Coherence transactions are point-to-point messages routed via the directory rather than broadcasts. The directory is itself distributed — each node owns the entries for the addresses in its local DRAM, and a physical address uniquely identifies its home — so there is no central bottleneck.
Compared to snoop-based coherence, directory protocols trade a level of indirection (3 hops instead of 2 for some transactions) for vastly reduced bandwidth — making them viable at hundreds of cores.

Three refinements make directory coherence practical. Its metadata is kept from scaling with memory by sparse directories; its multi-hop transactions force the protocol to reason about transient states and races; and workload-specific patterns like migratory sharing let it collapse pairs of transactions into one. See Implementing Directory-based MESI in Murphi for a full worked implementation in Murphi.

fr:title.text: Directory protocols expose transient states because transactions span multiple hops

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Directory protocols expose transient states because transactions span multiple hops

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Because a directory transaction takes several hops (requestor → home → owner → …), a line spends observable time in transient states between the stable ones — e.g. \mathrm {MI}^{A} ("modified, going to invalid, waiting on an acknowledgment"). These are not an implementation detail to wave away: concurrent transactions to the same line race, and the protocol must define a correct outcome for every interleaving. That combinatorial state space is what makes directory protocols hard to get right.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Example. L holds a dirty copy and starts a writeback to home H. Concurrently R sends a read to H. R sits in \mathrm {S}^{D} ("shared, waiting for data") until the race resolves.

Remark. Never resolve these races with NACKs — they cause starvation. The Implementing Directory-based MESI in Murphi Murphi implementation works through the channel-separation arguments that keep the transient-state space deadlock-free.

fr:title.text: Sparse directories keep coherence metadata from scaling with memory

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sparse directories keep coherence metadata from scaling with memory

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A directory must remember which caches hold each line, and the naive encoding — a sharer bitmap per cache line — does not scale: at 256 nodes that is 32 bytes of metadata per line, so roughly half of memory goes to coherence bookkeeping. Two ideas bring it back down. Limited-sharer encoding exploits the fact that most lines have ≤4 sharers: track those exactly and fall back to broadcast for the rare widely-shared line. Sparse directories go further and cache the directory entries themselves — an entry missing from the directory cache means nobody holds the line at all, and evicting an entry invalidates the corresponding lines. The directory then scales with the number of actively cached lines rather than with total memory.

fr:title.text: Snoop-based coherence keeps caches consistent by watching a shared bus

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Snoop-based coherence keeps caches consistent by watching a shared bus

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A Cache coherence family where every cache watches (snoops) a shared bus. When one cache issues a coherence transaction (e.g. requests permission to read or write a line), every other cache sees it and updates its local state accordingly. No central directory needed; the bus itself is the coordination mechanism.
The simplest snoop-based protocol is valid-invalid:

html:ul.html:li: Invalid + load → BusRd to gain read permission; transition to valid.
Invalid + store → no transition (write-through assumed; the bus carries the write).
Valid + store → BusWr to notify other caches; they invalidate.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Write-update coherence, the variant where stores update other caches' copies instead of invalidating them, works for very small bus-based systems but does not scale: every write reaches everyone, and copies of data the snooper isn't using pollute its Cache replacement policy.
Snoop-based coherence relies on a shared physical bus, which limits it to roughly 8 cores. Beyond that, switch to directory-based coherence.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Snoop-based SMPs use the Inclusion property so that snooping at L2 suffices — every L1 line is also tracked at L2.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In a Multicore system where every core has its own Cache hierarchy, the same memory address can live in multiple caches simultaneously. A cache coherence protocol is the mechanism that keeps those copies consistent — propagating writes, invalidating stale copies, and preserving two invariants:

html:ol.html:li: Single-writer invariant: at any moment, at most one core has permission to write a given line. No other core can read or write it concurrently.
Data-value invariant: all cores see the same order of updates to a given line.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two organizational families:

html:ul.html:li: snoop-based coherence — every cache watches a shared bus and reacts to other cores' traffic. Scales to ~8 cores.
directory-based coherence — a structure tracks who has a copy of each line; coherence messages are point-to-point. Scales to hundreds of cores at the cost of an extra hop.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The concrete state machines are protocols like MSI protocol, MESI protocol, MOESI protocol, and DEC Firefly, each adding states to handle more cases or to optimize specific sharing patterns. A worked implementation of directory-based MESI in Murphi lives in Implementing Directory-based MESI in Murphi.
Worked instance: Implementing Directory-based MESI in Murphi implements directory-based MESI in Murphi.

Murphi is an explicit-state model checker: you describe a system as guarded transition rules, state the invariants, and it enumerates every reachable interleaving looking for a violation. That makes it a natural fit for cache coherence, where the steady-state behavior is easy and the races are not. This post builds a directory-based MESI protocol in Murphi, starting from MSI and adding state every time the checker finds a way to break it.

The state tables come from A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence, which doubles as the source for these notes. The recurring lesson is that the published tables are not quite enough: every protocol below needs transient states the tables leave implicit.
Syntactical things I need to remember from Murphi docs. Most things are straightforward, but there are a few things to note:
A declaration is a variable or a collection of variables that are used in the rules.
A rule is a transition from one state to another

html:ul.html:li: Each rule can optionally have an initial condition required to be fired
We can easily define rules for all the processors or collection of n things with ruleset.
For our use case, rules are used to define

html:ol.html:li: Controller actions
Receiving a request from the network
Retrying stalled requests

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A startstate is the intial configuration for all our declarations.

html:ul.html:li: Must assign a value to every global variable

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An invariant is something that Murphi checks to ensure is true at all possible configurations of the system.
Overview straight from the docs. Repeat forever:

html:ol.html:li: Find all rules whose conditions are true in the current state. (i.e. conditional expressions are true, given the current values of the global variables).
Choose one arbitrarily and execute the action, yielding a new state.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The valid-invalid protocol shipped with the Murphi docs uses two Virtual Channels. A directory protocol needs three: one each for requests, forwarded requests, and responses. The reason is that deadlock is a cycle in the dependency graph, so it suffices to exhibit one.

html:ul.html:li: A node issues GetS to the directory, giving an edge N_1 \to D.
The directory forwards Fwd-GetS to the owner, extending the chain to N_1 \to D \to N_2.
The owner sends data back to the requester, closing the cycle N_1 \to D \to N_2 \to N_1.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The data closing that cycle would travel on the same channel as the requests waiting behind it, so a full request buffer wedges the response that would drain it. Partitioning by message class breaks the cycle:

html:ul.html:li: Request: GetS, GetM, PutS, PutM
Forwarded: Fwd-GetS, Fwd-GetM, Inv, PutAck
Response: Data, InvAck

fr:mainmatter.html:p: These are enumerated directly in the model's MessageType.
MESI is easier to reach through MSI, where there is less to get wrong and the races are already interesting enough.
The starting point is the primer's MSI cache controller table.

html:figure.html:figcaption: MSI cache controller. Rows are states, columns are events.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Several table entries are left blank; those are resolved at runtime from the AckCount, which is why the per-processor record carries an ack field alongside the state.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. load, store, and replacement only move the protocol between stable states. To simulate the system it is therefore enough to implement the rules that initiate those transitions — evict from modified, load from invalid — and let the model checker drive the transient states from there.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The directory side starts from the analogous table.
This table is where the first real gap shows up. It gives the directory a single transient state, and the races below force a second one, M^D.

fr:title.text: Losing data to a PutM/Fwd-GetM race

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Losing data to a PutM/Fwd-GetM race

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Consider the PutM rule that downgrades a cache from modified to invalid. The evicting cache must not drop the data when it sends PutM, because it may still have to service a forwarded request; it transitions to MI^A and keeps the value. But nothing stops the PutAck from arriving first, taking it to I before the Fwd-GetM shows up. The data is gone and the forwarded request has nobody to answer it.

Fix. Add the M^D state to the directory controller. While in M^D, a PutM from a node that is not the current owner stalls until the data arrives. Leaving M^D for M requires the new owner to send data back to the directory even on a three-hop transaction, so the directory learns that the forward actually completed. I have not found a cleaner way to close this race without the extra state.

fr:title.text: Deadlocking two stores against a load

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Deadlocking two stores against a load

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The M^D fix introduces a deadlock of its own. Take two processors that store-miss and a third that load-misses. The second store wins at the directory: the first store gets data and moves IM^{AD} \to IM^{A}, then the second triggers a Fwd-GetM that takes ownership away from it.

Meanwhile the load miss sits in IS^D. When its Inv arrives, the table says to stall — and because Inv and Fwd-GetM share the forwarded channel, that stall blocks the Fwd-GetM behind it. The winning processor never receives the data, and nothing ever drains the channel.

Fix. Another transient state absent from the table: II^A, meaning "was in IS^A, got invalidated, now waiting on PutAck before settling in I". The invalidation is processed rather than stalled, so the forwarded channel keeps moving.

fr:title.text: Not clearing the owner too eagerly

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Not clearing the owner too eagerly

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One more correction to the table: when the home directory is in M and receives a GetS, it must not clear the owner field as the figure directs. Once in S^D, the directory can no longer tell whether an incoming PutM came from the owner (and should stall) or from a stale node. The owner is only cleared once the data has actually arrived.
With those states in place the rest of MSI is mechanical, and MESI is a short step from it — modulo two design choices and two more races.

Silent upgrades. If a cache in E may upgrade to M silently, the directory never learns the line went dirty, and the value it hands to the next GetS or GetM is stale. There are two consistent ways out: forbid the silent upgrade, in which case no forwarding is needed; or allow it and treat E exactly like M, forwarding everything. Neither requires a writeback on PutE. I take the first, matching the table.

Signaling exclusivity. The directory needs a way to tell a requester "you are the first reader, take the line exclusive." That is a new ExclusiveData message: receiving it in IS^D lands the cache in E rather than S. It turns out to also be the key to the second race below.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Once PutE or PutM has been sent, EI^A and MI^A are functionally identical. Both appear above for completeness, but transitioning from E straight into MI^A verifies the same.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Symmetrically, the directory gains an E^D state, which for completeness is kept distinct from M^D but could be folded into it.

The first processor issues GetS and waits in IS^D, while the home directory has already moved to E and sent it ExclusiveData. A second processor then issues GetM, and home's Fwd-GetM overtakes the data in flight.
Fix. Stall Fwd-GetM and Fwd-GetS in IS^D until the data lands. This is safe here because the data is on the response channel, which no stall can block.

fr:title.text: Losing exclusive data to an invalidation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Losing exclusive data to an invalidation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The nastier version of the same race: the invalidation arrives before the forward. By the II^A rule inherited from MSI, a PutAck in that state drops the line to I — discarding data a forwarded request is about to ask for.

html:ol.html:li: Proc_1 load-misses → IS^D
Home takes the first GetS from Proc_1 → E, sends ExclusiveData
Proc_2 issues GetM → IM^{AD}
Home sends Inv to Proc_1
Home forwards Fwd-GetM to Proc_1
Proc_1 receives Inv → II^D
Proc_1 receives ExclusiveData → I, and the data is lost

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Fix. ExclusiveData pays for itself a second time. Because the message is distinguishable from ordinary Data, a cache receiving it in II^D knows it was the first reader and transitions to E instead of I — from which the pending Fwd-GetM or Fwd-GetS is handled correctly.
Folding all of the above in leaves these two state machines, which Murphi verifies exhaustively.

fr:title.text: Migratory-sharing optimization collapses read-then-write into one coherence transaction

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Migratory-sharing optimization collapses read-then-write into one coherence transaction

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A common access pattern is migratory: a core reads a line and then writes it — think a lock or a hand-off variable that passes from core to core. Handled naively this costs two cache-coherence transactions: a read miss that fetches the line shared, then a write miss that upgrades it to modified. Upgrade-miss detection spots the pattern and, on the read miss, transitions the line straight to a migratory-exclusive state, so the following write is silent — one transaction instead of two.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The same optimization hurts producer–consumer sharing, where one core writes and several read. There the right move on a read miss is to downgrade the previous writer rather than invalidate it, so later readers source the line from the last writer instead of racing to own it. The lesson generalizes: coherence optimizations are workload-shaped — a win for one sharing pattern is a loss for another.
